title: Chapter 49: Lilies, Part 5 of 5: Goodnight, Aunt
html:
She went down the stairs between the lilies.
She did not remember the corridor. She did not remember the white carpet, or the shut white doors, or the gallery at the top. She remembered the stairs. The two white curving arms of them, wound with lilies, going down into the gold haze of the hall. The heavy heads brushing her shoulders. The gold pollen falling. And her mother's gray slippers, one step, and then the next, and the next, the way she had been taught to walk at fourteen with a book on her head, while somebody counted.
She counted. Thirty-one steps.
At the bottom, he was waiting.
Not the Duke. She saw the Duke across the hall, on his white silk sofa by the door of the long room, with his cane across his knees and his eyes half shut. He saw her. His ringed hand lifted, a little, off the gold head of the cane.
But at the foot of the stairs, at the bottom of the white banister, between her and the Duke, standing quite alone, with a tall thin glass in his hand that he had not drunk from, a slight man in plain dark gray.
He was looking up at her.
The hall was full. A hundred people, more, talking, laughing, the soft roar of the sea in the shell. Nobody was near him. There was a space round him on the white marble, the way there was always a space round the white coats on the Ministry Steps. A clear round space, a little wider than his arms, that the crowd flowed round without seeming to know it was doing it.
Lyra came down the last step and stopped, because there was nowhere else to go.
"Lady Lyra," said Silas Kross.
His voice was soft and pleasant and a little tired. A schoolmaster's voice, at the end of a long term.
"Inquisitor."
"I won't keep you." He smiled. A small smile. Mild. Kind. His pale washed-out eyes rested on her face the way you rest your eyes on a picture you have heard a great deal about and are seeing, at last, for yourself. "I only wanted to say good evening. And that your brother speaks of you." A pause. "Not often. Not to me. But I hear him."
Lyra did not move.
"He's a good boy," said Kross. "A careful boy. He can fold eleven now. Did you know? He did it for the first time on Tuesday night, in the dark, with the lamp out." He turned the tall thin glass a little in his fingers. "He hasn't shown me. I expect he'll show me when he's ready."
He held out his other hand.
There was something in it. On the palm. Small. Wrapped in a twist of waxed paper.
A barley sugar.
"For the carriage," said Kross. "It's a long way down the Hill. And cold."
Lyra looked at it.
She did not take it.
She stood at the foot of her aunt's lily stairs in her mother's gray gown and looked at the barley sugar on the Inquisitor's open palm, and did not take it, and did not say anything. And after a moment, Kross smiled again, as if she had done something clever, and closed his hand, and put the sweet back in the pocket of his gray coat.
"Quite right," he said. "Never take sweets from strangers. Your mother would have said the same."
And then he did a thing she was not ready for.
He put the tall thin glass down on the white newel post at the bottom of the banister. Carefully. Among the lilies. And he laid his hand on the white wood beside it. Flat. The way her father laid his hand flat on the blanket in the hay.
And his first finger lifted.
And fell.
Four.
Lyra did not breathe.
Two.
The hall roared round them like the sea. Nobody was looking. Nobody saw. A slight man in gray, at the foot of the stairs, resting his hand on the banister while he talked to a girl.
Nine.
She felt her own finger move. Inside Madame Hesper's glove. At her side. She felt it want to. The way Moll had said his had wanted to, under the table, so much that he had to sit on it. The way Rowan's had, in the tower, on her hand. She felt it lift, a hair's breadth, inside the old white kid, against her gray silk skirt.
Three.
And stop.
And wait.
Lyra Thorne stood at the foot of the lily stairs with her hands at her sides and her chin up, just enough, and looked at the Inquisitor, and held her finger still with every single thing she had left.
She did not answer.
Kross waited.
He waited for a long time. She did not know how long. The music came through the white doors of the long room, slow and sweet and old, the tune she knew and could not name. The pollen fell. The sea roared. And his finger lay flat on the white banister, still, waiting, the way her father's lay in the hay.
Then he took his hand away.
And picked up his glass.
"Good night, Lady Lyra," he said pleasantly. "Do give my regards to Mister Vane. Tell him I hope his leg is mending." He smiled. "Tell him I'll see him on Monday."
He turned and went away across the white hall, through the crowd, which opened in front of him and closed behind him without seeming to know it was doing it. Toward the long room. Toward the fire.
Lyra stood at the foot of the stairs.
She found she could not move her hand. Her right hand. The one at her side. She had held it still so hard that it had gone stiff, and when she tried to open it, it would not open. She stood there with her fist clenched in Madame Hesper's glove against her mother's gray silk.
Then the Duke of Marrow was beside her.
She had not seen him get up. She had not heard him cross the hall. He was there, enormous, soft, breathing a little heavily, with his cane in one hand. And he did not say anything. He only took her clenched right hand in his own large soft ringed one, gently, the way you pick up a bird that has flown into a window, and put it through his arm. And held it there, under his own hand, against the dark blue velvet of his sleeve.
And walked her out.
Across the white hall. Past Lady Ashcombe in her chair, who watched them go with her small black eyes and, at the last moment, as the gray silk went by, very slightly, inclined her head. Past the great white urns. Past the footman in white, under the lily knocker, through the white door. Down the white steps, over the white felt, between the torches, to the carriage.
The cold hit her like water.
She breathed it in. All of it. Deep, into the bottom of her chest, so cold it hurt. Clean. Smelling of snow, and horses, and nothing else at all.
Tibbs had the door open. The Duke handed her in. Then it took a long time, and the carriage tipped and groaned, and then the Duke was in too, on the other side, with the gray fur rug over his knees and his feet across the floor. And the door shut. And the gray horses leaned into their collars, and the wheels hissed in the snow, and Number 11 slid away past the window, blazing, every window gold.
She did not look back.
They went along Crown Walk in silence. Past the dark house with its shut eyes and the pale square on its door and the stone girl kneeling on the top step with her jug full of snow. Lyra looked at it this time. Straight at it. Until it was gone.
Then the carriage turned, and began to go down the Hill.
And her right hand, in her lap, slowly, opened.
"Well," said the Duke of Marrow, in the dark.
Lyra did not answer for a long time.
"She pays the nurse," she said at last. "To write patient taps. So that nobody will listen. So that he'll be left alone." She looked at the window. "She says she's kept him alive. For two years."
"And did you believe her?"
"I don't know."
The Duke was quiet.
"Good," he said. "That's the beginning of wisdom, on the Hill. Not knowing, and saying so." The rings caught the light from a passing lamp. "And Lot Forty-one?"
"She's giving it away. No money. To whoever wants it most. In public. So that whoever takes it has to be seen taking it."
The Duke did not say anything to that. But in the light of the next lamp, Lyra saw his sleepy eyes come fully open. And stay open. And look at her, for a long time, the way they had not looked at her all night.
"And the Inquisitor," he said softly.
"He tapped," said Lyra. "At the foot of the stairs. On the banister." She looked down at her right hand in her lap. At Madame Hesper's glove. At the first finger, inside it. "And I didn't answer."
The carriage went down the Hill in the snow.
"No," said the Duke of Marrow, after a while. "I saw." He was quiet. "That was the bravest thing I have seen anyone do in that house in twenty years."
He did not go to sleep, this time. He sat in the dark with his ringed hands folded on the fur and his eyes open, all the way down the Hill, all the way through the High Quarter and the Ink Quarter and the narrow lanes behind the Corn Exchange, to the bottom of Comb Street.
Where, under the one gas lamp, in the snow, a big man in a too-short coat with his arm in a black sling was standing exactly where she had left him. With a boy beside him, small, in a white sling, sitting on the bottom step with his chin on his knees.
"He wouldn't come," said Gideon, when the carriage door opened. Flatly. "I tried at the tenth bell. He said he was counting."
Oren did not say anything. He looked at her face, as Tibbs handed her down onto the snow. And then down, at the snow at her feet, and back up at her face. Checking.
"Eleven," he said. "That was the eleventh bell. Just now. I counted."
"I know," said Lyra.
And took his good arm, the right one, and held it. Hard. With the hand that had not answered.
The Way Back
They walked back up Saint Bride's Hill in the dark, the three of them, in the snow.
The snow had nearly stopped. A few flakes still came down, slow and dry and small, out of a sky that had begun, here and there, to show black between the clouds. There was a star. One. Low over the river, very small, very white. Lyra looked at it as they climbed, because it was easier than looking at anything else.
Oren walked one pace behind her and one to the left. Gideon walked ahead, with his hands in his pockets and his sling across his chest, looking at every corner and every doorway and every dark mouth of every alley before they reached it, the way Oren had taught him on the way down. He did not need to be taught twice. He did not need to be taught anything twice.
Nobody said anything for a long time.
Then, at the corner of Chandler Row, where the WANTED posters were, soft and gray now under the wet, Lyra stopped.
She did not mean to. Her feet stopped. She stood on the corner in her coat with the gray silk showing under it and looked at the posters, and at the new one beside them with the paste still shining. A GENTLEMAN from the Office will be IN PERSON at the FISH STAIRS. Somebody had torn it, today, across the middle. A long angry rip, from the top corner to the bottom. And under the rip, on the wall, in chalk, in big crooked letters, somebody had written a word.
FEVER.
Lyra looked at it for a long time.
"What does it say?" said Oren behind her. Very low.
She told him.
He was quiet. Then he said, "Good."
They went on.
"Oren," said Lyra, after a while.
"Lady."
"When my mother went away. To the coast." She did not turn round. "You rode with her. To the gate."
"To the city gate." His voice did not change. "She told me to go home."
"Which gate?"
Oren did not answer at once.
"The east one," he said. "By the old customs house. Where the river road goes out toward the salt flats." He paused. "Not the west one. Not the coast road." Another pause. "I didn't think about it. Not for eleven years. I thought about it yesterday, in Hesper's shop, when she said about the wool dress. And the Narrow Sea."
"Lady Ashcombe gave her the name of a smuggler," said Lyra. "A month before. A ship's captain. Who went east across the Narrow Sea in winter."
Oren stopped walking.
Lyra heard him stop. She stopped too, and turned round. He was standing in the middle of the snowy street with his good hand at his side and his face, in the light of a window, gone very still.
"What name?" he said.
"Fey. Captain Fey. Of the Lantern."
Oren did not say anything for a long time.
Then he said, slowly, like a man feeling for a step in the dark: "There was a ship. That winter. At the salt flats. Not a ship. Not a boat." He frowned. "Something in the sky. I saw it, from the gate, as I turned the horse for home. Over the flats, very far off, low. Like a long dark fish. With a light under it." He looked at her. "I thought it was a cloud. I thought my eyes were tired. I never told anyone. Who would I tell?"
Lyra stood in the street and looked at him.
And neither of them said anything else, all the rest of the way up the hill.
Corin was awake.
He was sitting up on his stone bench under the skulls, with the Ledger open on his knee and the lamp on the floor, exactly as she had left him. As if he had not moved in four hours. Perhaps he had not. He looked up as she came in under the arch in her coat and her mother's gown, and his eyes went down to the page of faces, and up again, and his mouth went down at the left corner.
And then he saw her face, properly, and it stopped.
"Tell me," he said.
She told him.
She sat down on the floor by the bench, in the gray silk, with her back to the cold stone wall, the way she had sat there every night that week. And told him all of it. In order. The way Juno told things, but slower. The Duke in the dark. Crown Walk and the shut house and the stone girl. The hall of lilies. Lady Ashcombe and her stick. Fey. Captain Fey. Of the Lantern. The silver hair, and the watch he did not look at. He's just seen that you didn't wear his present. The white room. The cups. The nurse. So that he would be left alone. The card with the plum seal. Proceeds: none. The three men who had come to the white chair. The lily paper, and her aunt's face when she smelled it. She stays—
And then the pins.
Corin did not move while she told him that part. He sat on the bench with his gray hand flat on the open Ledger and his eyes on her face, and did not move at all. Not when she counted the pins out loud for him. Five. Not when she told him about the loose place in the gold hair, low on the left. Not when she told him what her aunt had said by the fire.
Yes.
There were things in that scribe's head about your sister, darling. And I could not let anybody else have them.
When she had finished, the vault was very quiet.
Oren was standing in the arch. He had not sat down. Gideon was sitting on the floor by the blue chalk shapes, with his knees drawn up, looking at them. Bet was asleep. Out in the long low hall, the children breathed.
"Pell Dorran," said Corin at last.
His voice was very low.
"He ran four steps," said Corin. "In the lane. In the Ink Quarter. I've had his last minutes in me since the autumn. Some of them. A big man's hand. Beer and onions. A lantern swinging." He looked down at the Ledger. "And a white shell mask, bending over him. With a silver cup. I've seen it every time I shut my eyes for three months. I never saw the face behind it."
"Now you know."
"Now I know." He closed his gray hand on the page. "And she says she did it for you."
"For my sister," said Lyra.
The word lay there in the vault between them.
Sister.
She had not said it out loud before. Not to him. Not to anyone. She had thought it, on the long walk up the hill, behind Gideon, under the one white star. She had thought it in the tower, and at the pump, and on the barge, for weeks, without letting herself know she was thinking it. A third chair against the nursery wall. A scratched cup. A height chart with a name gouged out. I remember there were never any others.
"I don't know who she is," said Lyra. "I don't know where she is. I don't know if she's alive. Cressida wouldn't say. She said it was the one thing in the city a man with a dome on his ring was still afraid of." She looked at her hands in her lap. Madame Hesper's gloves. "She said, as long as nobody says it out loud, he stays afraid, and she stays— And then she stopped."
Corin looked at her for a long time.
Then he opened the Ledger. Not to the back, where the lists were. To a page near the front. An old one. In ink that had gone brown with time. Lyra knew it. She had read it, in the autumn, on the floor of Vespera's shop. A page with a drawing on it. A tree. An oak. And under the tree, in his square capitals, a few lines about a green book in a doctor's careful hand. W. Brought by H.L. himself. Wrapped in a soldier's coat. Aged about two. Registered. Bright.
And beside it, pressed flat, a leaf.
Not the real one. A drawing of one. In pencil. Rounded lobes, soft deep curves going in and out along the edges, like waves.
"I made a promise," said Corin slowly. "In the autumn. To somebody. In writing." He turned the Ledger round on his knee so that she could see the line, underlined twice. I promised Wren Halloway I will tell her what I know about the oak leaf. FIRST. Before anyone. As soon as I am sure. "I'm not sure," he said. "I'm not. But I'm a good deal less unsure than I was this morning."
Lyra looked at the line.
She thought of a girl in white, who she had never met, sitting in an attic full of black books. A girl of twenty-two. Two years older than Lyra. Who hummed three notes while she copied, and did not know she was doing it. The whole Long Office stopped yesterday to listen to her, Rowan had said. I knew the notes. The first three.
It's hers. Isn't it. Mother's.
Lyra put her hand over her mouth.
She did not know why. Nobody was going to hear her. She sat on the floor of the side vault of the crypt of Saint Bride's, in her mother's gray gown, with her hand over her mouth, and looked at the drawing of an oak leaf in Corin's Ledger. And the vault was very quiet. And from the long hall outside, very faint, the children breathed.
"Monday," said Corin softly.
She took her hand away.
"Monday," she said.
The Health's carts, at Saint Bride's, before the Midwinter bells. The Masquerade, under the dome, at the ninth bell. A white mask with a clock in it. A door marked with a V and a 3. A box with a folded square on its clasp. An Inquisitor and a girl in white in the gallery. A Treasurer with a watch he did not look at. A sealed bid, and midnight.
And somewhere in the middle of all of it, a girl who hummed the beginning of their mother's song, and a man who knew the rest.
"Three days," said Corin.
"Two and a half."
He looked at her. And his mouth went down at the left corner.
"You're counting," he said.
"I always count," said Lyra Thorne. "Now more than ever."
And on the floor beside her, in the lamplight, the four blue chalk shapes that a boy had drawn for a man who could not read lay where they had been all evening. A boot. A fork. A gate with a belly. A tent. Nobody had swept them away. Lyra looked at them for a long time before she slept, and thought that she had never, in all her life, seen her own name look so much like a promise.
